name: Hana Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Hana, and thanks for this. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to any company, union or party, and what you tell me is confidential. What does a normal day at work look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm line lead on bottling line two at Cascada Drinks, the soft drinks plant by the river. The line fills and caps about twenty thousand bottles an hour, and my job is keeping it running: changeovers between flavours, clearing jams at the labeller, and chasing faults on the filler. I've got a crew of five on days. Most of my day is listening for the sound of something about to go wrong.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how do you chase a fault?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Half by feel and half by my phone, honestly. The filler is run by a PLC, that's the little computer that tells every valve when to open, and it throws error codes that the manual explains badly. I take a photo of the screen and ask an AI app what it means and what to check first. I do that every day now, and it's saved me hours. The engineers upstairs think I'm cheating; I think they're slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype. I'd be a bit disappointed, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was always going to be more useful on the shop floor than the adverts said, and less magic. Online I'd probably post that the real story is still who owns the factories and what they pay. I'd say the union should stop worrying about robots and go after the wage freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I'm still the best line lead on the lowest wage band, in a town with two factories. My rent went up sixty this year and I've got about two weeks of money in the account. AI saving me ten minutes on a fault doesn't touch my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI app for faults and teach my crew to do it too, so they don't ring me at home. I'd apply for the maintenance technician trainee spot the next time it comes up, because it pays a band higher. And I'd look at a cheaper flat share with my partner Sam.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless. Not scared, just stuck in second gear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at a cheaper flat. What would that mean for you and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A smaller place further out, probably above the shops on Mill Road. Sam works at the bike repair place in town and would hate the longer ride. But sixty a month is sixty a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you gone for the maintenance trainee job before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It came up once and they gave it to a man with less time on the line than me. I didn't fight it. I would now.

say: AI was always more **useful than magic**, and less than the adverts said.
The union should drop robot fears and fight the **wage freeze**.
think: She's still the **best line lead** on the lowest wage band.
Rent rose **sixty** this year and she has about two weeks saved.
do: Teach her crew to use the **AI app** for filler faults.
Apply for the **maintenance trainee** role at a higher band.
Look for a **cheaper flat** with Sam on Mill Road.
feel: **Restless** and stuck in second gear, though **not scared**.
S0.quote: AI saving me ten minutes on a fault doesn't touch my rent.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** and treats it as a plain tool.
Her stress is **rent and pay**, not the technology.
She was passed over once for **maintenance** and now says she would fight for it.

steps.text: Train her five-person crew to read filler faults with the AI app
Apply for the next maintenance technician trainee opening
Move with Sam to a cheaper flat on Mill Road

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one feels most like what's already happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the union to bargain for training, not just pay. Out loud I'd say: the robots are coming slowly, so let's make sure the people on the line are the ones who learn to fix them. I'd post that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a good spot if I move now. My line is hands-on, so the robots take a while, and I'm already the one who uses the AI tools. The person I worry about is Teresa in the planning office, who's been doing the schedule on a spreadsheet for twenty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the maintenance trainee role straight away. I'd start an online PLC course at night, the free one from the college, and use the AI to quiz me. And I'd offer to help Teresa learn the new planning software, because she helped me when I started.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, a bit guilty that it's good for me and not for others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm twenty-seven and I like screens. Teresa in planning is fifty-four and doesn't like screens. Same factory, totally different future, and that's not fair on Teresa.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong for you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cascada could decide to buy a fully automatic line from a supplier who sends their own technicians. Then my new skills are worth less here, and there's only one other factory in town.

say: Unions should bargain for **training**, not just pay.
The people on the line should be the ones who **learn to fix** the robots.
think: She's in a **good spot** if she moves now, with robots arriving slowly.
She worries about **Teresa in planning**, who has used spreadsheets for twenty years.
do: Apply **straight away** for the maintenance trainee role.
Take the college's free **PLC course** at night, using AI to quiz herself.
Help **Teresa** learn the new planning software.
feel: Mostly **good**, with some **guilt** that it favours her and not others.
S1.quote: Teresa in planning is fifty-four and doesn't like screens. Same factory, totally different future, and that's not fair on Teresa.
fieldNote: She sees herself as a likely **winner** here and feels guilty about it.
Her one real fear is Cascada buying a line with **supplier technicians**.
Progressive views show in her urge to **help colleagues** and push training bargaining.

steps.text: Apply now for Cascada's maintenance technician trainee role
Take the college's free online PLC course at night
Push the union to bargain for paid robot-repair training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a different feeling entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it publicly: this is what governments are for. If AI can do every thinking job in two years, we need public income support and a big training programme, paid by the companies getting rich from it. I'd be organising, not just posting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think even fault-finding is thinking work, so in 2028 the AI does that better than me. Then in 2031 the robot does the hands-on part. My whole plan to move into maintenance has maybe a three-year shelf life. That's scary, because I don't have money to wait it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd learn everything about the robot systems Cascada might buy, so I'm the one who installs them. I'd start fixing coffee machines and bikes with Sam on weekends for cash, because hands-on repair lasts until 2031 at least. And I'd get the union to set up a hardship fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but awake. Like when the line stops and you have ninety seconds before the bottles back up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a three-year shelf life. What happens in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe I'm one of the few people who supervises the robots. Maybe there's no job like that. I'd rather be in the room working it out than outside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Eating out, which isn't much. Then the phone contract. I'd keep the internet, because that's my classroom.

say: Governments must provide **income support** and big training paid by the companies.
think: AI does **fault-finding** better than her by 2028.
Her move into **maintenance** has maybe a three-year shelf life.
do: Learn the **robot systems** Cascada might buy, to be the installer.
Fix **coffee machines and bikes** with Sam for weekend cash.
Get the union to set up a **hardship fund**.
feel: **Anxious** but **awake**, like a line stop with ninety seconds to act.
S2.quote: My whole plan to move into maintenance has maybe a three-year shelf life.
fieldNote: She sees that **fault-finding** is thinking work and goes first, which most operators miss.
She stays in **problem-solving** mode, unlike colleagues who freeze.
Thin cushion pushes her to **side income** with her partner.

steps.text: Learn the robot palletiser systems Cascada is likely to buy
Repair coffee machines and bikes with Sam on weekends
Organise a union hardship fund for line workers
Cancel the phone contract and eating out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Long enough to do something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have five years and no excuse. I'd push for a regional training centre, run with the union and the college, so people like my crew can learn robot work before 2034. I'd go to council meetings for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to get a proper qualification, maybe the two-year automation diploma. But the thinking AI arrives in 2031, and that changes how robots get fixed too. I'd be training for a job that's half gone by the time I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the automation diploma part-time next September. I'd ask Cascada to pay half, in return for staying three years. And I'd keep using the AI every day, since by 2031 working alongside it is the skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a thread of worry running through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said half gone. Why train for it, then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the half that's left is the part with hands in it. Somebody still has to climb inside the filler and swap a valve until the robots can. That's my three extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to start learning now, not in 2030. Lewis on my crew says he'll wait and see. I'd tell Lewis that waiting is a choice too.

say: Five years means **no excuse** for being unprepared.
Push for a **regional training centre** with the union and the college.
think: Five years is enough for the **automation diploma**.
By 2031 thinking AI changes repairs, so the training may be **half gone**.
do: Start the **automation diploma** part-time next September.
Ask Cascada to **pay half** in return for staying three years.
Keep using **AI every day** as a working skill.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a thread of **worry** through it.
S3.quote: Somebody still has to climb inside the filler and swap a valve until the robots can.
fieldNote: She sees the **hands-on half** of maintenance as her three-year buffer.
She pushes **crewmates** to act early and calls waiting a choice.
Wants **shared costs**: employer funding tied to staying on.

steps.text: Start the part-time automation diploma next September
Ask Cascada to pay half the fees for a three-year stay
Lobby the council for a regional robot training centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's a whole career change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, with nobody left behind. I'd want a public plan, every factory, every worker, a training place and a wage while you learn. I'd say that everywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's mostly good. I'd finish the diploma, get into maintenance, maybe even move to a bigger plant in the city, and be an expert by the time the robots come. My worry is the money in the meantime, not the end point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the cheap stuff this year: the online PLC course and the maintenance trainee job. I'd save twenty a month in a course fund. In about three years I'd look at moving to the city with Sam for better pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. Like I've been given a map.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said moving to the city. Would Sam go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam would go if there's a bike shop, and there's always a bike shop. My mum would cry, though. She's twenty minutes away now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make this harder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Cascada closed early to save money before the robots even come. That happens. Then the ten years doesn't matter, it's next month that matters.

say: Ten years is enough to do this **fairly**, with **nobody left behind**.
She'd want a public plan with a **wage while learning**.
think: The end point looks **good** for her, finishing the diploma and becoming an expert.
Her worry is **money in the meantime**, not 2039.
do: Start the **PLC course** and the maintenance trainee job this year.
Save **twenty a month** in a course fund.
Plan a **move to the city** with Sam in about three years.
S4.quote: My worry is the money in the meantime, not the end point.
fieldNote: The long warning makes her **optimistic** about her own path.
She still names an **early closure** of Cascada as a live risk.
Moving away from her **mother** is the personal cost she flags.

steps.text: Start the online PLC course and maintenance trainee job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even the skills I'm building go stale fast and I have no savings to bridge it. What would help is a wage while you train, paid for by the companies, and the union having a real seat when Cascada buys robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask who gets trained first. In my experience it's the men who drink with the managers. If the training goes to the same people as always, the robots just make the old unfairness faster.

headlineQuote: If the training goes to the same people as always, the robots just make the old unfairness faster.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old** line lead on a bottling line at Cascada Drinks.
She uses **AI daily** to decode filler fault codes and is impatient with slow engineers.
Lower-paid with about **two weeks saved**, she lives with her partner Sam, a bike mechanic.
She aims to move into **maintenance and automation**, and backs union-led training.
Only the **two-year** warning really shakes her plan; longer ones feel like a map.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, when her new skills go stale with **no savings** to bridge.
whatWouldHelp: A **wage while training**, paid by companies.
The union having a **real seat** when Cascada buys robots.
